articles.headline: Our cities are not built for the heat they now face
articles.standfirst: Heat action plans have saved lives. But a city where millions sleep under tin roofs and work in the open sun needs more than advisories and water kiosks.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a construction worker resting in the thin shade of a scaffold under a white-hot sky.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a labourer sheltering from harsh sun on a building site.

body.value:
There is a particular kind of silence that settles over an Indian city at three in the afternoon in May. Streets empty, shutters come halfway down, and the only people still out are those who have no choice: the construction worker on the eighth floor of an unfinished tower, the traffic constable, the woman selling cut fruit under a plastic sheet, the delivery rider racing a ten-minute promise. For them, the heat is not weather. It is a working condition.

We have become better, in some ways, at responding to it. Ahmedabad's heat action plan, the first of its kind in South Asia, showed more than a decade ago that early warnings, hospital preparedness and simple public messaging could reduce deaths during heatwaves. Dozens of cities and states now have similar plans, encouraged by the National Disaster Management Authority, and the India Meteorological Department issues heat warnings with far greater accuracy and lead time than it once did. These are real achievements, and the people who built them deserve credit.

But a heat action plan is, at heart, an emergency protocol. It tells people when to take shelter and tells hospitals when to expect patients. It does not change the fact that a family in a one-room tenement with a tin roof has no cool place in which to shelter, or that a daily-wage worker who stops between noon and four loses a third of the day's wage. It does not cool the city.

value.quote: A heat action plan tells people to stay indoors. It does not ask what indoors is like.

body.value:
Three changes would make a larger difference. The first is to treat heat as a labour issue. Several states have issued advisories asking employers to shift outdoor work away from the hottest hours, but advisories are not enforceable, and those who ignore them face no penalty. A binding rule on working hours during declared heatwaves, with compensation for lost hours for the lowest-paid, would protect people far better than a poster asking them to drink water. Some women's cooperatives have experimented with insurance that pays out automatically when temperatures cross a threshold; such schemes deserve public support and wider trials.

The second is to build differently. Cool roofs — a coat of reflective paint, or a modular insulating layer — can bring indoor temperatures down by several degrees at very low cost. Telangana has adopted a cool-roof policy, and pilot programmes in Ahmedabad and elsewhere have shown what is possible. Building codes, which still treat heat as an afterthought, should require passive cooling in new construction, and slum-upgrading programmes should take roofs as seriously as toilets.

The third is to plan for shade and water as public goods. Our cities have been paving over lakes and felling trees for road-widening for decades, and every one of those decisions has made the city hotter. Restoring tree cover along streets where people walk and wait, protecting water bodies, and keeping public drinking-water points working through the summer are not luxuries. They are infrastructure.

None of this is glamorous, and none of it fits neatly within a single department. Heat falls between the cracks of urban development, labour, health and disaster management, and so it is everyone's problem and nobody's responsibility. Some have argued that heatwaves should be formally notified as a disaster, which would unlock dedicated funds. That would help, but only if the money goes into prevention rather than relief after the fact.

Climate projections leave little doubt that hot days will become hotter and more frequent across much of India. We can keep responding to each summer as if it were a surprise, counting the dead and issuing advisories. Or we can start designing cities in which the people who keep them running can survive the afternoon.

articles.headline: Consent is not enough: the flaw at the heart of India's data protection rules
articles.standfirst: The new data protection regime asks individuals to read, understand and police how their data are used. That is a burden few can carry, and the law should not pretend otherwise.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a hand hovering over an endless scroll of privacy terms on a phone screen, with an 'I agree' button at the bottom.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a phone showing a very long privacy notice and an agree button.

body.value:
Somewhere in the settings of your phone are dozens of permissions you granted without reading: to a food-delivery app, a bank, a ride-hailing service, a game your child downloaded. Each came with a privacy notice you scrolled past. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the rules that put it into effect, each of those taps is meant to carry legal weight. That is the problem.

The law is a genuine step forward. For the first time, Indians have a statutory right to know what personal data a company holds about them, to have it corrected or erased, and to complain to a Data Protection Board if their rights are violated. Companies that suffer breaches must report them, and penalties for failures can run into hundreds of crores. Children's data receive special protection, with verifiable parental consent required before processing. After years of drafts and delays, these are not small things.

But the architecture of the law rests on consent, and consent, as it operates online, is something close to a fiction. Studies of how people interact with privacy notices consistently find that almost nobody reads them, and that those who try rarely understand them. A regime that treats a tick in a box as informed agreement places the burden of protection on the individual — the party with the least information and the least power in the transaction.

value.quote: We do not ask passengers to inspect the engine before boarding a plane. Why do we ask users to audit a data processor before opening an app?

body.value:
The rules attempt to address this with “consent managers”: registered intermediaries through which users can give, review and withdraw consent across services. The idea has merit, and India's experience with account aggregators in finance shows that such intermediaries can work. But consent managers make consent easier to manage, not more meaningful. If the choice is between agreeing to broad data use and not using a service at all, a better interface does not change the choice.

What is missing is a stronger set of obligations that apply regardless of consent. Well-regarded data protection laws elsewhere lean heavily on principles such as purpose limitation and data minimisation, which require companies to collect only what they need for a stated purpose and to use it only for that purpose. The Indian law gestures at these ideas, but the weight of enforcement falls on whether consent was obtained, not on whether the processing was reasonable.

Two other features deserve scrutiny. The first is the breadth of the exemptions available to the government. The state is the largest processor of personal data in the country, through its identity, welfare, tax and health systems, and the law allows the Centre to exempt its agencies from many obligations on grounds such as security and public order. Exemptions are not unusual in such laws, but they should be narrow, time-bound and subject to independent oversight.

The second is the Data Protection Board itself. Its members are appointed by the government, and its independence will depend heavily on how it is staffed and funded. A regulator that must adjudicate complaints against government departments needs to be visibly separate from them. Journalists and transparency campaigners have also warned that the law's amendment to the Right to Information Act could make it easier for officials to refuse information by citing privacy.

None of this is an argument against the law. It is an argument for treating it as a beginning. The rules will be revised; the Board will issue decisions; courts will interpret its ambiguities. At each of those points, the guiding question should be whether protection depends on what an ordinary person can reasonably be expected to do. If it depends on reading privacy policies, it will not protect anyone.

articles.headline: Mumbai's lifeline needs more than automatic doors
articles.standfirst: Closing the doors on suburban trains will save some lives. The deaths will not stop until the railways tackle the crush that pushes people to the edge in the first place.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a crowded Mumbai suburban train at a platform, commuters packed into the open doorway.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of an overcrowded local train with passengers at the door.

body.value:
Anyone who has taken a Mumbai local at 9.15 in the morning knows the choreography. You wait at the exact spot on the platform where the door will stop. You brace as the train pulls in, still moving. You are carried in by the crowd behind you, or you are not carried in at all, and you hang from the door frame with one hand and your bag clutched in the other, the wind tugging at your shirt as the train leans into a curve.

For millions of Mumbaikars this is not an adventure. It is the commute. The suburban network carries upwards of 70 lakh passenger journeys on a typical weekday, on rakes designed for a fraction of that load. The cost is measured in lives. For years, railway police records have counted deaths on the suburban tracks in the thousands every year — people falling from overcrowded trains, crossing tracks where no bridge exists, struck in the dark. The toll has declined from its worst, but every few months a single incident reminds the city how fragile the system remains.

After the most recent such tragedy, the railways said new suburban rakes would come with automatic doors, and that existing non-air-conditioned rakes would be retrofitted where possible. This is welcome. Closed doors will prevent some falls, and there is no good argument for running trains with open doors in this century. But we should be clear about what automatic doors can and cannot do.

value.quote: A closed door keeps people inside the train. It does nothing for the people left on the platform.

body.value:
On the busiest routes at peak hours, the crowd on the platforms of major stations already exceeds what a train can absorb. Doors that close will mean more people left behind, longer waits and heavier crowding on platforms and foot-overbridges, which carry risks of their own. Ventilation in non-AC trains with closed doors must be redesigned, or the cure will be worse than the disease in a Mumbai May. And none of this addresses deaths while crossing tracks, which have long made up a large share of the toll.

The real problem is capacity, and capacity is a decades-long project. Successive phases of the Mumbai Urban Transport Project have added lines, longer trains and new rakes, but implementation has repeatedly lagged behind schedule. Additional corridors to separate suburban from long-distance traffic, modern signalling that lets trains run closer together, and more fifteen-car services would each raise the number of people the system can carry safely. These are not new ideas. They have sat in reports for years.

There are cheaper levers too. Staggered office timings, which state and central government offices in the city could adopt tomorrow, would flatten the peak. Fencing and foot-overbridges at known crossing points would save lives at little cost. Better integration with the metro lines now opening across the city could draw passengers away from the most crowded stretches — but only if fares, ticketing and interchanges are designed for people switching modes, rather than as separate systems that happen to meet.

Air-conditioned trains, which come with automatic doors, deserve a word. They are popular with those who can afford them and resented by those who cannot, particularly when they replace ordinary services rather than adding to them. Safety should not become a premium product. Whatever is done must be done on the trains that most people actually ride.

Mumbai has learned to live with its local trains the way one learns to live with a chronic condition: with stoicism, humour and an elaborate set of coping habits. That resilience is admirable. It should not be mistaken for consent. The people who hang from the doors every morning are not taking a risk they chose. They are taking the only train there is.

articles.headline: Let Parliament do its homework
articles.standfirst: A crowded legislative agenda is no excuse for skipping scrutiny. Committees exist to slow good bills down just enough to make them better.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a committee room with members seated around a horseshoe table, bound reports stacked before them.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a parliamentary committee meeting around a horseshoe-shaped table.

body.value:
The government arrives at the monsoon session with a long list of bills and a short calendar. The opposition arrives with its own list of grievances. If past sessions are any guide, the outcome is predictable: days lost to adjournments, followed by a rush in the final week in which bills are passed in minutes, sometimes by voice vote amid protest. Both sides will then blame the other. Both will be partly right.

The casualty is scrutiny, and it is worth being precise about why that matters. Most laws are not passed to make headlines. They are technical instruments — on insolvency, cooperatives, shipping, the repeal of obsolete statutes — whose effects depend on definitions, exceptions and the powers they grant to officials. Errors in such details tend to surface years later, in courtrooms and in the lives of the people the law was meant to help. By then, correcting them requires another bill.

Parliament has a mechanism designed to catch those errors: its committees. Department-related standing committees and select committees can examine a bill clause by clause, take evidence from experts and affected groups, and propose amendments away from the theatre of the floor. Their proceedings are not televised, which allows members to change their minds without losing face. Many committee reports are models of careful, cross-party work.

Yet the share of bills referred to committees has fallen sharply over the past two decades, according to data compiled by PRS Legislative Research. Governments of different stripes have found it convenient to bypass a step that takes time and can produce awkward recommendations. That is a mistake, and not only on principle. Bills that have been through committee tend to be better drafted, command broader support and are less likely to be challenged in court.

value.quote: A committee referral is not a delay. It is quality control.

body.value:
We would urge three things this session. The government should refer at least the more complex bills on its list to committees, even at the cost of passing them in a later session. The opposition should allow question hour and legislative business to proceed, and use the debates it has demanded to argue its case rather than to disrupt. And the presiding officers should use the discretion the rules give them to send bills to committees where the government does not.

None of this is beyond reach. Parliament has worked better than this in the past and can again. The legitimacy of a law rests not only on the number of votes it receives but on the quality of the deliberation that produced it. Voters are entitled to expect that their representatives have read what they are voting for.

articles.headline: Bengaluru's water warning is meant for every city
articles.standfirst: The city's new rules on borewells and tankers are necessary. But the crisis they respond to is the product of decades of planning that treated water as someone else's problem.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a dried, cracked lake bed with apartment towers rising on its former shoreline.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a dry lake bed surrounded by high-rise buildings.

body.value:
Bengaluru's water board has announced rules to meter borewells, regulate private tankers and require builders to use treated wastewater. These are sensible measures, and overdue. But they are also an admission. A city that pumps much of its drinking water uphill from a river roughly a hundred kilometres away, and fills the gap by drilling ever deeper into a falling water table, has been living beyond its means for a long time.

The story is not unique to Bengaluru. Chennai's taps ran dry within recent memory. Delhi's poorer neighbourhoods depend on tankers every summer. Smaller cities growing at breakneck speed, from Telangana to Gujarat to the Gangetic plain, are reproducing the same pattern: development first, pipes later, groundwater in between.

That pattern has three features. Cities expand faster than their piped networks, so new neighbourhoods are built on borewells and tankers, which then become entrenched interests. The natural infrastructure that once stored and recharged water — lakes, wetlands, flood plains, open ground — is lost to construction, often with official sanction. And water is priced and measured so poorly that nobody, from the utility to the household, has an accurate picture of how much is used and how much is lost.

Each of these can be addressed. Metering, which Bengaluru is now extending to borewells, is the foundation: what is not measured cannot be managed. Treated wastewater, which most Indian cities still discharge into rivers and drains, can replace fresh water for construction, industry and landscaping on a large scale. Protecting and restoring water bodies is cheaper than building new reservoirs, and it reduces flooding in the monsoon — the other half of the urban water problem.

value.quote: A city that cannot account for its water cannot claim to manage it.

body.value:
The harder part is political. Water tariffs that reflect even a fraction of the cost of supply are unpopular; enforcement against errant tanker operators and illegal borewells antagonises powerful interests; protecting lakes means saying no to builders. Municipal bodies that have gone without elected councils for long periods, as many have, are especially poorly placed to make those choices with legitimacy.

None of this argues for waiting. Smart metering, wastewater reuse and lake restoration can begin within a single budget cycle, and they pay for themselves many times over in avoided tanker bills and flood damage. What they require is a municipal leadership willing to be accountable for water as a whole, rather than for pipes alone.

Bengaluru's new rules are a start. Every other growing city should read them not as a local story but as a forecast — and act before its own taps run dry.

about_page.title: About & AI policy
about_page.intro: The Ledger is an analysis-led publication about India and its place in the world. We publish news, analysis, explainers, opinion and editorials, and we care more about context than speed. Please note that the site is currently running demonstration content: the articles and authors you see are illustrative examples written to show how the publication works, not reports of real events.

body.value: Who we are

The Ledger is an independent newsroom built on a simple idea: that readers are better served by understanding a story than by merely hearing about it first. We cover politics, the economy, cities, society, education, health, science and India's relations with the world, and we try to explain not just what happened but why it matters and what might happen next.

We are a small team of reporters, editors and columnists drawn from across the country. We have no affiliation with any political party, and our editorial decisions are made by our editors alone.

value.title: Demonstration content
value.body: This site currently runs demonstration content. Bylines belong to fictional writers, people quoted are illustrative, and articles are written to show our formats and standards rather than to report specific real events. Real institutions are mentioned for context only, and nothing here should be cited as fact.

body.value: Our editorial standards
Every article we publish is reviewed by at least one editor before it goes live. We hold ourselves to a few non-negotiable principles:

value.title: Our principles
points: Accuracy first: we check facts, figures and quotations before publication, and we say so when something cannot be verified.
Clear sourcing: we link to primary documents and official data wherever possible, and list our main sources at the end of each article.
Fairness: people and organisations we write about critically are given a reasonable opportunity to respond.
Anonymity is the exception: we grant it only when a source would face real harm for speaking, and we describe their role as precisely as we can.
Separation of news and opinion: our reporting does not take sides; our opinion pages and editorials are clearly labelled.

body.value: Article types

Every article carries a label so that you know what kind of journalism you are reading.

  • News reports what has happened, as fully and fairly as we can establish it.
  • Analysis goes behind the news to explain causes, consequences and trade-offs. It reflects the reporter's informed judgement but not a political position.
  • Explainer sets out the background to a complex subject, often in question-and-answer form, so that readers can follow the debate.
  • Opinion is a signed argument by a columnist or guest writer. It represents the writer's view, not The Ledger's.
  • Editorial is the unsigned, collective view of our editorial board, and the only place where The Ledger itself takes a position.
Our AI policy
We use artificial intelligence as a tool, in limited and clearly defined ways, and never as a substitute for reporting or editorial judgement.

value.title: What this means in practice
points: AI may assist with transcription of interviews, summarising long documents such as reports and judgments, producing first drafts of translations, and checking data for errors and inconsistencies.
AI never writes our opinion columns or editorials.
We never use AI to generate photographs or images presented as real. Illustrations are labelled as illustrations.
Every article in which AI tools played a material role carries an “AI-assisted” badge and a short note explaining how they were used.
A human editor reviews everything we publish and is accountable for it, whatever tools were used along the way.

body.value: We review this policy regularly as the technology and our understanding of it change. If you believe an article falls short of these standards, we want to hear from you.
Corrections

We make mistakes, and when we do we correct them promptly and transparently. Corrections are noted at the foot of the article concerned, with a description of what was changed. Minor fixes to spelling or style are made without a note. To report an error, write to corrections@example.com with a link to the article and a description of the problem.
